AIs coming up with their own questions, hypotheses, and then testing those systematically is the next leap forward. Most AI usage is reactive currently and not pro-active.

The article highlights that as part of the reasoning chain, the AI actually made some connections that are interesting to historians by themselves and raise new questions. Good science is as much about finding these new interesting things to explore as it is about resolving problems. > There’s a growing sense in the AI community that we’re approaching an intelligence explosion far faster than even the most optimistic accelerationists predicted.

This might concern those worried about losing their jobs to AI. But it should concern AI companies as well. AI is rapidly approaching the point of diminishing returns--after solving the world’s most challenging problems, how much room is left for improvement?

Once AI becomes "good enough" for almost any task, investments in AI could be at risk. That's because AI has little inherent moat: you can swap Claude for an OpenAI model and get comparable results. Open-weight models are not far behind, and they may eventually catch up. Meanwhile, hardware is becoming more powerful and cheaper. A machine capable of running inference with a frontier model might cost $500,000 today, but comparable capability could become available on a $5,000 machine in a few years.

If people can run an open-weight model as powerful as today's frontier models on a $5,000 machine, AI companies could face severe pressure on both revenue and profit margins.

It's a very narrow kind of problem that historians, archivists and literary scholars occasionally have to work on--establishing provenance, authorship, etc. on particular documents and manuscripts held within archives, and using a form of forensic analysis to establish possible connections between texts about which we know less than we might like.
